headline: SDCC compiler deep dive for 8051 microcontrollers
summary: Explore how SDCC transforms C code into binaries for 8051 microcontrollers, detailing registers, peripherals, and instruction sets.
details: This article delves into the inner workings of the SDCC compiler, specifically focusing on its application with 8051 microcontrollers. By disassembling the generated binary and comparing it to the original C source code, developers can gain a deeper understanding of the compilation process.

The standard 8051 microcontroller features a compact 4KB ROM and 128 bytes of RAM, making efficient use of every byte crucial. The architecture includes four 8-bit I/O ports, two 16-bit timer/counters, and a flexible interrupt system supporting five distinct sources for real-time event handling.

The 8051 instruction set, while rudimentary, is highly direct, consisting of 111 instructions using 255 opcodes. These instructions, along with various addressing modes, form the basis for operations like decimal adjustments for BCD values.

In contrast, modern architectures like x86_64 boast thousands of instruction variations, including extensive extensions like MMX and AVX. Their opcodes can span multiple bytes, requiring more complex hardware decoding compared to the single-byte base opcodes of the 8051.

A unique feature of the 8051 is its Special Function Registers (SFRs), directly mapped into the memory space from 0x80 to 0xFF. This allows direct access to core hardware registers like the Stack Pointer (SP) and Accumulator (ACC) using their hex addresses or mnemonic names, streamlining low-level hardware control.

headline: YouTube doubles monetization requirements for new creators starting Feb 1
summary: New partners will need 8,000 watch hours or 20 million Shorts views to join the YouTube Partner Program.
details: YouTube is significantly raising the bar for new content creators looking to monetize their channels. Starting February 1, 2023, aspiring partners will need to meet much higher watch hour or Shorts view thresholds. The subscriber count remains at 1,000, but the watch hour requirement doubles from 4,000 to 8,000 over the past year.

For creators focusing on short-form content, the challenge is even steeper. The requirement for Shorts views will jump from 10 million in the last 90 days to a staggering 20 million. This change aims to ensure creators have a substantial audience before they can start earning ad revenue.

Existing partners are also subject to new rules. They must maintain either 1,000 watch hours annually or 1 million Shorts views. However, this can be avoided by consistently uploading content, specifically two long-form videos or five Shorts every 90 days. Creators who remain inactive for six months will be removed from the program.

YouTube justifies these changes by highlighting the expansion of its YouTube Premium Lite subscription to more countries. The company suggests that this ad-free viewing option, which excludes music streaming, will bring in more subscribers and thus increase earnings for creators. They claim Premium Lite viewers contribute to a better revenue pool.

However, the actual impact of Premium Lite on creator earnings remains uncertain. YouTube has not disclosed specific subscriber numbers for this tier, though it reports a combined 125 million paid users across all its subscription services globally. This contrasts with YouTube's massive monthly user base of nearly 2.7 billion.
